# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS: CUTANEOUS LESIONS</mark>

<mark>The clinical presentation of Cushing syndrome may be subtle.</mark> <mark>Skin findings are often present, and when carefully correlated with systemic complaints, they can lead to an early diagnosis.</mark> <mark>Common skin manifestations include easy bruisability and skin thinning.</mark> <mark>Mild hypertrichosis, typically of the lanugo type, and acne may also occur.</mark> <mark>Frank hirsutism and severe acne suggest the possibility of a concurrent androgen-secreting tumor.</mark>

<mark>The development of multiple violaceous striae wider than $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ on the abdomen or proximal extremities is highly suggestive of Cushing syndrome.</mark> <mark>The width and violaceous color of these striae help differentiate them from the narrower, hypopigmented striae commonly seen in pregnancy or with rapid weight gain.</mark>

<mark>Relatively dramatic changes in fat distribution often accompany generalized weight gain.</mark> <mark>There is increased central adiposity with thinning of the extremities.</mark> <mark>Central obesity, along with facial fat accumulation, leads to a rounded facial appearance known as **moon facies**, often accompanied by facial erythema and telangiectasias.</mark> <mark>Additional fat deposition occurs in the dorsocervical region (buffalo hump) and supraclavicular fossae.</mark> <mark>Men may develop **gynecomastia**.</mark>

<mark>Although uncommon, **hyperpigmentation** can occur in Cushing syndrome, particularly when there is marked overproduction of ACTH—most often from an ectopic source, but sometimes from the pituitary.</mark> <mark>Both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC), contribute to increased melanin production, similar to what is seen in Addison disease.</mark>

<mark>**Acanthosis nigricans** may be present due to insulin resistance associated with Cushing syndrome, which often leads to diabetes mellitus.</mark> <mark>The immunosuppressive effects of excess glucocorticoids predispose patients to increased **dermatophyte and candidal infections** of the skin and nails.</mark>

<mark>Women may present with **irregular menses or amenorrhea**.</mark> <mark>Other systemic features include **hypertension, osteoporosis, muscle wasting, and proximal muscle weakness**.</mark>

---

# TABLE 152-11  
**Approach to the Patient with Cushing Syndrome**

## <mark>Cutaneous findings in Cushing syndrome</mark>
- <mark>Increased central adiposity (moon facies and buffalo hump) with thinning of the extremities</mark>  
- <mark>Skin thinning and easy bruisability</mark>  
- <mark>Violaceous striae</mark>  
- <mark>Acanthosis nigricans</mark>  
- <mark>Increased dermatophyte and candidal skin and nail infections</mark>  
- <mark>Rarely, hyperpigmentation</mark>  

## <mark>Related features</mark>
- <mark>Diabetes</mark>  
- <mark>Hypertension</mark>  
- <mark>Osteoporosis</mark>  
- <mark>Irregular menses</mark>  

## Diagnosis
- Measurement of cortisol in serum and urine  
- Failure to suppress cortisol production with dexamethasone suppression tests  

## Management
- Appropriate endocrine and surgical consultation  
- Surgical removal of pituitary or adrenal adenoma  
- Adrenal enzyme inhibitors  
- Radiation therapy  

---

# LABORATORY TESTS

Diagnostic confirmation of Cushing syndrome requires demonstration of excess cortisol production. Cortisol levels exhibit diurnal variation, typically peaking in the early morning. Therefore, serum cortisol should be measured at 8 A.M.

The average daily cortisol production can be assessed via **24-hour urinary free cortisol** measurement. Any abnormal result should be confirmed with repeat testing (two to three times).

If urinary or serum cortisol levels are elevated, the diagnosis is supported by **failure to suppress** cortisol during a **low-dose dexamethasone suppression test** (e.g., 1 mg overnight or 2 mg over 48 hours).

Further testing, such as the **high-dose dexamethasone suppression test**, helps differentiate pituitary-dependent Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH production or adrenal tumors.

It is important to note that **hypercortisolism** can be present in the absence of true Cushing syndrome (e.g., in pseudo-Cushing states such as obesity, depression, or alcoholism), so careful clinical correlation is essential.

# Dermatoscopic findings

They consist of white crossing lines (Wickham sign), dull red background, and peripheral arrangement of vessels.

# Other assays

It has been proposed that future diagnostic adjuncts could include cytokine profiling of involved tissue. However, as other available tests are reasonably accurate for the diagnosis of LP, this is unlikely to become a widely used assay for LP.  

Patch tests in patients with LP usually reveal positive results, which are not associated with specific variants of cutaneous LP or the prognosis of the disease. Patch testing is better to be included in the workup of oral LP, where oral lesions show proximity to dental restorations. The material of these restorations can aggravate or induce the lichenoid reaction.  

No imaging studies are necessary for the diagnosis of lichen planus.

# Differential diagnosis

There are many disorders to be considered in the differential diagnosis of lichen planus:

- Lichen nitidus, lichen sclerosus, lichen spinulosus, graft-versus-host disease, lichen striatus, linear epidermal naevus, naevus unius lateralis  
- Eczema, lichen simplex chronicus, prurigo nodularis  
- Pityriasis rosea, guttate psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, eczematid-like purpura  
- Drug eruption, syphilis, tinea corporis, papular acrodermatitis of childhood  
- Granuloma annulare, lichen amyloidosus, pityriasis lichenoides, Kaposi sarcoma

# Clinical variants of lichen planus

Several variations have been described, according to (i) the distribution and configuration of lesions, (ii) the morphology of an individual lesion, and/or (iii) the site of involvement. The various clinical forms are divided into three general categories: cutaneous, appendageal, and mucosal lichen planus, as well as some unclassified other forms of LP (Table 2). More information about the clinical variants is available in the longer version on the EDF homepage.

# Complications

## Acute complications

Itching is most common in cutaneous LP. In oral LP, eating might be so painful that patients are unable to maintain adequate nutrition. Oral lichen planus and the drugs used for treatment may predispose to infection from *C. albicans*. Sexual dysfunction may also occur and can become a long-term complication in genital erosive lichen planus.

## Chronic complications

After resolution of lichen planus lesions, the affected skin area often develops postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, which is more noticeable in individuals with darker skin.

## <mark>Hyperpigmentation in Various Conditions</mark>

Pre-existing pigmented lesions such as **nevi** and **ephelides** become darker during pregnancy. <mark>Also, recent scars often darken.</mark> <mark>In normally pigmented areas such as the **nipples**, **areolae**, and **genitalia**, the pigmentation becomes more intense.</mark> <mark>The **linea alba**, the median line on the anterior abdominal wall, often becomes hyperpigmented during pregnancy and is then called **linea nigra**.</mark> <mark>In a small proportion of pregnant women, hyperpigmentation occurs in the **axillae** or the **inner upper thighs**.</mark> **Melasma**, or "mask of pregnancy" (see the section Melasma), occurs in more than 50 percent of pregnant women (see Chap. 107).

### Acanthosis Nigricans
**Acanthosis nigricans** is associated with hyperpigmentation and is discussed in Chaps. 152 and 154.

### Diabetes
(See Chap. 153) A higher **vitiligo** prevalence has been reported in patients with **diabetes type I and II** compared to the general population. **Diabetic dermopathy** is characterized by asymptomatic, irregular, light brown, depressed patches on the anterior lower legs, but the pathogenesis is not known.

### Nutritional Conditions
(See Chap. 130) Pigmentary changes can be secondary to nutritional conditions such as **kwashiorkor**, **vitamin B₁₂ deficiency**, **folic acid deficiency**, or **pellagra**. The skin changes are reversible upon correction of the nutritional deficiency.

### <mark>Metabolic Conditions</mark>

#### Porphyria Cutanea Tarda
**Porphyria cutanea tarda** is a metabolic disorder associated with diffuse brown hypermelanosis, accentuated in sun-exposed areas. In females, a melasma-like facial hyperpigmentation can be observed (see Chap. 132).

#### Hemochromatosis
**Hereditary hemochromatosis** is an autosomal recessive disorder associated with increased intestinal absorption of iron and deposition of excessive iron in the liver, pancreas, and other organs, including the skin. In the past, hemochromatosis was typically diagnosed at an advanced stage by the classic triad of **hyperpigmentation**, **diabetes mellitus** ("bronze diabetes"), and **hepatic cirrhosis**. Skin darkening was present in 70% of patients, due to two mechanisms:  
- **Hemosiderin deposition**, causing a diffuse slate-gray discoloration  
- **Increased melanin production**, causing a bronze hue  

Because hemochromatosis is now usually diagnosed earlier, hyperpigmentation is less frequently observed. The pigmentation is typically generalized but may be more pronounced in sun-exposed areas, genitalia, and scars. Skin bronzing is reversible once phlebotomy therapy is initiated.

### Tumoral Conditions

#### Mast Cell Disorders
Mast cell disorders can lead to hyperpigmentation and are discussed in Chap. 150.

#### Melanoma
(See Chap. 124) **Diffuse generalized melanosis** associated with advanced metastatic melanoma is a rare but well-documented event. It is characterized by a slate bluish-gray to brown discoloration of the skin. Histology reveals melanin particles and melanin-containing histiocytes and dendritic cells in the dermis and subcutaneous fat. No melanoma cells are detected in the skin, and there is no increase in epidermal melanin or melanocyte number. Circulating melanosomes have been detected in the blood, supporting the hypothesis that diffuse melanosis may result from tumor lysis with release of melanosomes into the circulation and subsequent deposition in the skin.

### Physical Agents

#### Ultraviolet Radiation
The major acute effects of UV radiation on normal human skin are **sunburn**, followed by **tanning** (see Chap. 89).

#### Ionizing Radiation
(See Chap. 95) Exposure of the skin to ionizing radiation—such as in nuclear accidents (e.g., Chernobyl) or after local fractionated radiotherapy—can lead to **cutaneous radiation syndrome**, characterized by fibrosis, keratosis, telangiectasias, and sharply demarcated lentiginous hyperpigmentation resembling UV-induced lentigines.

# DISORDERS OF THE ADRENAL GLAND

## <mark>Cushing Syndrome</mark>

<mark>Excessive production of endogenous cortisol manifests clinically as **Cushing syndrome**.</mark> <mark>Similar clinical findings can also result from chronic exogenous administration of glucocorticoids.</mark> In normal physiology, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis regulates cortisol production: corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to produce corticotropin (ACTH). ACTH is derived from a larger precursor molecule called proopiomelanocortin (POMC). POMC is cleaved into several biologically active peptides, including melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) and ACTH. ACTH then stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol. Cortisol exerts negative feedback on both the hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing further CRH and ACTH release.

### EPIDEMIOLOGY, ETIOLOGY, AND PATHOGENESIS

The overall incidence of Cushing syndrome is approximately 10 cases per million people per year, with a higher prevalence in women.

Cushing syndrome is categorized into two main types based on etiology:

1. <mark>**ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome**:</mark>
   - Most commonly caused by a pituitary microadenoma secreting excessive ACTH, known as **Cushing disease**.
   - Less commonly, **ectopic ACTH production** occurs, typically associated with neuroendocrine tumors such as pulmonary carcinoid tumors, though other malignancies may also be responsible.

2. **ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome**:
   - Results from autonomous overproduction of cortisol by the adrenal cortex, independent of pituitary regulation.
   - Causes include:
     - Adrenal adenoma (benign or malignant)
     - Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
     - Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (as part of **Carney complex**)
     - McCune-Albright syndrome

### CLINICAL FINDINGS: CUTANEOUS LESIONS

The clinical presentation of Cushing syndrome can be insidious. <mark>Cutaneous manifestations are common and may provide early diagnostic clues when correlated with systemic symptoms.</mark>

Key skin findings include:

- **Easy bruisability** and **skin atrophy** due to collagen loss
- **Thin, fragile skin** with a translucent appearance
- **Mild hypertrichosis**, often of lanugo-type hair
- **Acne**, which may be moderate to severe
- **Hirsutism** and **severe acne** suggest possible coexisting androgen excess, raising suspicion for an androgen-secreting adrenal tumor
- <mark>**Violaceous striae**: wide (>1 cm), purple or reddish-purple striae on the abdomen, thighs, or proximal extremities — highly suggestive of Cushing syndrome (Fig. 152-15)</mark>

<mark>Careful evaluation of these dermatologic signs in the context of systemic features (e.g., central obesity, hypertension, glucose intolerance, moon facies, proximal muscle weakness) can facilitate early diagnosis.</mark>

# PRIMARY CUTANEOUS T-CELL LYMPHOMAS

Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs) are non-Hodgkin lymphomas characterized by a dominant skin-homing T-cell clone. They account for approximately 80% of all cutaneous lymphomas. The most common subtypes are mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS), with an annual incidence of three to four new cases per million people. After MF and SS, the primary cutaneous CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorders—including lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) and primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (cALCL)—represent the second most common group of CTCLs, comprising approximately 30% of cases.

An understanding of the unique epidermal sanctuary that harbors, preserves, and perpetuates CTCL is essential for comprehending disease persistence and recurrence.

# <mark>Mycosis Fungoides</mark>

## <mark>DEFINITION</mark>

<mark>Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most frequent variant of CTCL, typically presenting in mid to late adulthood (median age at diagnosis, 55 to 60 years), with a male-to-female ratio of 2:1.</mark>

## <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Skin Signs</mark>

<mark>MF is clinically categorized into patch, plaque, and tumor stages, although patients may exhibit more than one type of lesion simultaneously.</mark>

### <mark>Patch Stage</mark>
<mark>In early patch-stage MF, patients present with single or multiple erythematous, scaly macules and patches of variable size, usually well-demarcated.</mark> <mark>Lesion color ranges from orange to dusky violet-red.</mark> <mark>The distribution typically favors non-sun-exposed areas, with early involvement of the "bathing trunk" region and intertriginous zones.</mark> <mark>The eruption may be intensely pruritic or asymptomatic and can occasionally be transient, resolving spontaneously without scarring.</mark>

<mark>Diagnosis at this stage is often challenging.</mark> <mark>Many patients report a history of "chronic dermatitis" lasting 10 to 20 years, previously misdiagnosed as contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, or eczema.</mark> <mark>In any case of therapy-resistant dermatosis, multiple skin biopsies should be performed to evaluate for MF.</mark>

### <mark>Plaque Stage</mark>
<mark>Patches may persist for months or years before progressing to plaques, or plaques may arise de novo.</mark> <mark>Plaques are sharply demarcated, scaly, elevated lesions that are dusky red to violaceous and variably indurated.</mark> <mark>Annular, arcuate, or serpiginous configurations with central atrophy and active disease at the periphery are characteristic.</mark> <mark>Central clearing may occur, leaving poikiloderma—comprising atrophy, telangiectasia, and pigmentary changes (hyper- or hypopigmentation).</mark>

### <mark>Tumor Stage</mark>
<mark>Tumors may develop anywhere but show a predilection for the face and body folds—such as the axillae, groin, antecubital fossae, and, in women, the inframammary area.</mark> <mark>Tumors may arise within pre-existing patches or plaques, indicating a vertical growth phase.</mark> <mark>This transition reflects more biologically aggressive behavior, with neoplastic cells expanding vertically through the dermis, leading to rapidly enlarging nodules or tumors.</mark>

## Staphylococcal Bacteremia in HIV Disease

Staphylococcal bacteremia may complicate either primary or secondary cutaneous infections such as psoriasis or scabies. However, the most common source of hematogenous dissemination is an intravenous catheter, accounting for 73 percent of bacteremia cases. <mark>As with most infections in HIV disease, staphylococcal infections are frequently recurrent.</mark>

Management (see Chap. 177) should include:
- <mark>Treatment of the acute infection</mark>
- Management of underlying dermatoses
- Eradication of nasal *S. aureus* carriage using mupirocin (pseudomonic acid) ointment
- Long-term oral prophylaxis for recurrent infections

---

## *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* Infections in HIV Disease

*Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (see Chap. 180) can cause primary cutaneous infections such as cellulitis (e.g., ecthyma gangrenosum), catheter-site infections, and secondary infections of underlying skin conditions like Kaposi sarcoma in advanced HIV disease.

Cutaneous *P. aeruginosa* infection occurs via:
- Local invasion through skin breaches
- Primary infection of skin appendages in the anogenital or axillary regions
- Hematogenous dissemination to the skin

These infections may progress to bacteremia, leading to seeding of multiple organ systems.

---

## Tuberculosis and Other Mycobacterial Infections in HIV Disease

Tuberculosis is the most common opportunistic infection in HIV-infected individuals in developing countries. While cutaneous tuberculosis (see Chap. 184) is relatively uncommon, the incidence of extrapulmonary tuberculosis is higher in HIV-positive individuals:
- 15% in non-HIV-infected individuals
- 20% to 40% in those with HIV disease
- Up to 70% in advanced HIV disease

Non-tuberculous (environmental) mycobacteria reported to cause cutaneous lesions in HIV disease include:
- *M. chelonae*
- *M. fortuitum*
- *M. kansasii*
- *M. malmoense*
- *M. gordonae*
- *M. marinum*
- *M. haemophilum*

The most common non-tuberculous mycobacterial pathogen in advanced HIV disease is the *M. avium-intracellulare* complex (MAC). However, MAC rarely presents with cutaneous manifestations. The incidence of MAC infection has declined due to primary prophylaxis with azithromycin and, more recently, effective antiretroviral therapy (HAART).

---

## <mark>Bacillary Angiomatosis and Bacillary Peliosis in HIV Disease</mark>

<mark>Bacillary angiomatosis (BA) and bacillary peliosis (see Chap.</mark> <mark>182), caused by *Bartonella henselae* and *B.</mark> <mark>quintana*, occur predominantly in the setting of advanced HIV-induced immunodeficiency.</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Features of Bacillary Angiomatosis</mark>

- <mark>Angioproliferative skin lesions resembling:</mark>
  <mark>- Cherry hemangiomas</mark>
  <mark>- Pyogenic granulomas</mark>
  <mark>- Kaposi sarcoma</mark>
- <mark>Cutaneous lesions are red to violaceous, dome-shaped papules, nodules, or plaques</mark>
- <mark>Lesion size ranges from a few millimeters to 2–3 cm in diameter</mark>
- <mark>Dermal vascular lesions with thinned or eroded epidermis</mark>
- <mark>Subcutaneous nodular lesions may also occur, sometimes lacking the typical red appearance</mark>
- <mark>Lesions are soft to firm and may be tender</mark>
- <mark>Number of lesions varies from solitary to over 100; in rare cases, more than 1000</mark>

<mark>Currently, the prevalence of BA in North America and Western Europe is very low, largely due to improved immune function from HAART and prophylactic strategies targeting opportunistic infections.</mark>

## <mark>Skin Involvement in Disseminated Infection</mark>

<mark>The skin is involved as a focus in one-third of cases with disseminated infection.</mark> <mark>More rarely, the skin is the primary location of infection.</mark>

<mark>Several types of skin lesions have been described, including:</mark>
- <mark>Abscesses with sinus tract formation</mark>
- <mark>Subcutaneous nodules with pustules</mark>
- <mark>Mycetoma</mark>
- <mark>Sporotrichoid nodules</mark>
- <mark>Cellulitis</mark>

Diagnosis is based on the demonstration of Gram-positive, partially acid-fast, branching bacilli in tissue or tissue exudate, or by tissue culture—although organism growth often takes several weeks. The treatment of choice is **trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole**. Other effective antibiotics include **minocycline**, **carbapenems**, and **amikacin**. Transplant patients may require long-term prophylactic therapy to prevent recurrence. Incision and drainage of cutaneous abscesses should also be performed.

---

## <mark>Bacillary Angiomatosis</mark>

<mark>Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by *Bartonella henselae* or *B.</mark> <mark>quintana* and typically occurs in AIDS patients and other immunocompromised individuals.</mark> Cutaneous lesions appear as painful, dome-shaped vascular papules and nodules, often resembling pyogenic granulomas. Disseminated infection can involve the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and brain. A history of cat scratches or bites is common, as cats are the natural reservoir for these bacteria.

Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying pleomorphic bacilli in tissue specimens using Warthin-Starry silver stain. <mark>Preferred treatments include oral **erythromycin** or **doxycycline**.</mark>

---

## <mark>Other Bacterial Infections</mark>

**Cellulitis** caused by *Streptococcus pyogenes*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, or *Staphylococcus aureus* may progress rapidly and lead to **necrotizing fasciitis** in immunosuppressed patients. Solid organ transplant recipients may develop recurrent cellulitis at the elbow—termed "transplant elbow"—often attributed to staphylococcal infection.

Individuals with complement deficiencies (particularly of late-phase components C5–C9) or alcoholism are susceptible to *Neisseria meningitidis* infection. These patients present with acute septicemia, meningitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and widespread petechiae and purpura.

Patients with underlying liver disease (e.g., alcoholic cirrhosis or hemochromatosis) are at risk for *Vibrio vulnificus* infection, a Gram-negative bacillus found in seawater and seafood. Infection occurs via ingestion of contaminated shellfish or through skin inoculation from seawater exposure. Clinical presentation includes rapidly progressive septicemia and painful cellulitis, bullae, or ulcers—typically on the lower extremities.

*Capnocytophaga canimorsus*, a commensal organism in dog and cat saliva, is transmitted through bites or scratches. High-risk hosts include alcoholics, asplenic individuals, and those on glucocorticosteroids. Skin manifestations include macules, papules, purpura, and gangrene. In immunosuppressed patients, *Salmonella enteritidis* has been associated with cutaneous abscesses of the head and neck.

---

## Fungal Infections

### Candidiasis

Although mucocutaneous candidiasis is less severe than disseminated disease in the context of acute immunosuppression, it is the most common complication in individuals with chronic cell-mediated immune dysfunction. Approximately 10% of patients with such immune impairment develop clinically significant mucocutaneous candidiasis.

# Unidentified Bright Objects (UBOs)

<mark>UBOs may be found in the internal capsule, basal ganglia, cortex, cerebellar hemispheres, optic tract, or brainstem.</mark> They do not enhance and are not associated with compression of surrounding tissue, features that distinguish them from neoplasms. <mark>UBOs are present in approximately 60 percent of children with NF-1 but disappear with age and are uncommon in adults.</mark> They are not associated with focal neurologic signs and are of uncertain significance. Histopathologic studies have shown that the UBOs correspond to areas of myelin vacuolization with increased water content. <mark>Some studies have found that children with NF-1 who have UBOs have significantly lower IQ and language scores, show significantly impaired visual-motor integration and motor coordination, and are at much greater risk for impaired academic achievement compared with NF-1 patients without UBOs.</mark>

# Intelligence and Learning Disabilities

Contrary to gross misstatements in the older literature, the mean IQ of patients with NF-1 is only 5 to 10 points lower than that of the general population and unaffected siblings. However, learning disabilities, defined as discrepancies between ability (intellect) and performance, are quite common, with an estimated prevalence of 30 percent to 60 percent. Although earlier reports suggested there might be a specific "cognitive phenotype" in NF-1 characterized by an excess of visual-perceptual disabilities, more recent studies have demonstrated that verbal deficits (e.g., reading) are at least as common as nonverbal disabilities in individuals with NF-1. These learning disabilities are lifelong and can affect adult functioning. Many children with NF-1 also have poor attention and impulse control and may be diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, which significantly interferes with school performance and learning. The use of stimulant medications may have a profound beneficial effect on the ability of these individuals to succeed academically and professionally.

# Treatment of Neurofibromatosis Type 1

Individuals with NF-1 are best cared for within a multidisciplinary clinic that has access to a wide range of subspecialists. The exact physician composition of the clinic is less important than the ability to obtain expeditious subspecialty consultation. All first-degree relatives should be examined for the cutaneous manifestations of NF-1 and should undergo slit-lamp examination at the first visit to ascertain the presence of Lisch nodules. <mark>Yearly visits allow the physician to identify NF-1 complications early while providing counseling and dissemination of information regarding NF-1.</mark> Individuals and families can obtain further information from the websites of the two national support groups, the Children's Tumor Foundation (http://www.ctf.org) and Neurofibromatosis, Inc. <mark>(http://www.nfinc.org).</mark>

All children with NF-1 who are 10 years of age or younger should have yearly complete ophthalmologic examinations to look for signs of an optic pathway tumor (OPT). These examinations should include assessment of visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields, as well as funduscopy and slit-lamp examination. <mark>Because almost all OPTs arise in children in this age group, the frequency of ophthalmologic examinations can be reduced in children older than 10 years of age.</mark> Yearly measurements of weight and height should be plotted on standardized growth charts, because the earliest indication of precocious puberty may be accelerated linear growth. Blood pressure measurements should be obtained at each visit to look for signs of renovascular hypertension. In addition, the spine should be examined each year for early signs of scoliosis.

# Café-au-Lait Spots

Café-au-lait spots on the face are unusual in individuals with NF-1. On occasion, they do occur, and affected individuals may seek to improve cosmesis. Attempts to remove café-au-lait spots with laser therapy have provided very mixed results. Although total disappearance of the lesion may be achieved, some studies cite a recurrence rate as high as 67 percent. Although results with use of the Q-switched ruby laser (694 nm) have been mixed, favorable reports in a limited number of cases using either the continuous-mode copper vapor laser (511 nm) or the erbium:yttrium-aluminum-garnet laser (2940 nm) have been published. Multiple treatments of a single lesion may be more effective.

# Cutaneous Neurofibromas

Discrete cutaneous neurofibromas may be removed surgically to improve cosmesis or to prevent local irritation (e.g., from brushing for lesions in the hairline or from rubbing against the shoe for those on the foot).

# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

A consensus development conference was held by the National Institutes of Health in 1987 to establish diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), with the goal of improving clinical research and patient care. <mark>The conference identified seven diagnostic features (Table 142-1), and it was recommended that two or more of these criteria be present to establish a diagnosis of NF-1.</mark> These criteria have proven highly effective and remain in use without modification more than 20 years later.

## Café-au-Lait Spots

<mark>Café-au-lait spots are flat, pigmented macules and are often the first clinical manifestation of NF-1 (Fig.</mark> 142-1). They are frequently present at birth and tend to increase in number during infancy and early childhood, with new spots commonly appearing throughout the first decade of life. As the child grows, existing spots also enlarge proportionally. Although they can occur anywhere on the body, they are rarely found on the face. The size, shape, and borders of café-au-lait spots are not diagnostically predictive; however, most spots in NF-1 are oval with smooth, well-defined margins.

The commonly cited notion that smooth-edged café-au-lait spots suggest NF-1 while irregular borders are more typical of McCune-Albright syndrome can be misleading and should be interpreted cautiously (Box 142-1). When café-au-lait spots overlap, the area of overlap may appear darker than either individual spot. When located within mongolian spots, they are often surrounded by a lighter pigmented halo.

The number or distribution of café-au-lait spots does not correlate with disease severity in NF-1. Additionally, the location of these macules does not predict where neurofibromas will develop.

Histologically, café-au-lait spots consist of clusters of heavily pigmented melanocytes of neural crest origin in the epidermis. These cells may contain increased numbers of "giant" melanosomes or melanin macroglobules, but these findings are not specific to NF-1 and have no diagnostic utility in biopsy specimens.

### TABLE 142-1 Diagnostic Criteria for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF-1)<sup>a</sup>

- Six or more café-au-lait macules >5 mm in greatest diameter in prepubertal individuals or >15 mm in postpubertal individuals  
- Two or more neurofibromas of any type, or one plexiform neurofibroma  
- Freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions  
- Optic pathway glioma  
- <mark>Two or more iris Lisch nodules</mark>  
- A distinctive osseous lesion, such as sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of the long bone cortex, with or without pseudarthrosis  
- A first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or offspring) with NF-1 by the above criteria  

<sup>a</sup> Two or more criteria required for diagnosis.

### Box 142-1  
**Differential Diagnosis of Syndromes Associated with Multiple Café-au-Lait Spots<sup>a</sup>**

- Neurofibromatosis type 1  
- Familial café-au-lait spots  
- LEOPARD syndrome (multiple lentigines, electrocardiographic abnormalities, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, abnormalities of the genitalia, growth retardation, deafness)  
- Neurofibromatosis type 2  
- McCune-Albright syndrome (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia)  
- Tuberous sclerosis  
- Fanconi anemia  
- Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B  
- Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome  
- Bloom syndrome  
- Ataxia-telangiectasia  

<sup>a</sup> Listed in approximate order of typical number of café-au-lait macules.

# THE NEUROFIBROMATOSES

# AT A GLANCE

<mark>Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), an autosomal dominant condition, occurs at an incidence of 1 in 3000 live births.</mark> <mark>Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2), a separate autosomal dominant disorder, occurs at an incidence of 1 in 40,000 live births.</mark>

<mark>NF-1 can be diagnosed clinically if two of the following features are present:</mark>  
- <mark>Six or more café-au-lait spots (larger than 0.5 cm in children, larger than 1.5 cm in adults)</mark>  
- <mark>Intertriginous freckling</mark>  
- <mark>Two or more cutaneous neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma</mark>  
- <mark>Optic nerve glioma</mark>  
- <mark>Characteristic bony lesion</mark>  
- <mark>Iris Lisch nodules</mark>  
- <mark>A first-degree relative with NF-1</mark>  

<mark>Cutaneous neurofibromas are softer than the surrounding connective tissue and protrude just above the skin surface or lie just under the skin.</mark> <mark>Subcutaneous neurofibromas, which arise from peripheral nerves and can be located under the skin or deep in the viscera, are generally much harder.</mark>

<mark>Plexiform neurofibromas, typically present at birth or evident within the first few years of life, may cause disfigurement, blindness (due to amblyopia, glaucoma, or proptosis), loss of limb function, or organ dysfunction through compression of vital structures.</mark> <mark>These individuals appear to have an increased risk of facial dysmorphism, mental retardation, early appearance of neurofibromas, and the presence of plexiform neurofibromas.</mark> <mark>There is evidence that NF-1 is more severe when inherited from the mother rather than the father.</mark>

The hallmark of NF-2 is the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas. Individuals with NF-2 are also at increased risk for developing multiple meningiomas, schwannomas, gliomas, and neurofibromas throughout the neural axis.

Segmental NF-1 involves manifestations of NF-1—typically café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas—limited to one region of the body. This results from a post-zygotic mutation in the *NF1* gene, leading to somatic mosaicism.

# Molecular Biology

The *NF1* gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 17 and encodes a protein called **neurofibromin**. Homozygosity for mutant *NF1* alleles has not been reported, likely because it is a lethal condition.

*NF1* has an unusually high mutation rate, estimated at $2.4$ to $10 \times 10^{-5}$ gametes per generation—one of the highest rates among known inherited disorders. This may be due to the large size of the gene, which spans $350\ \text{kb}$ of genomic DNA and contains 59 exons encoding a protein of over 2800 amino acids. Alternatively, the gene may have structural features that make it particularly prone to mutation.

New mutations account for approximately 50% of NF-1 cases and occur most frequently on the paternally inherited allele. Unlike many other autosomal dominant disorders, the frequency of new mutations does not increase with advancing paternal age.

Most *NF1* mutations lead to reduced intracellular levels of neurofibromin, which is sufficient to cause the clinical features of the disease. Tumorigenesis—such as the development of benign dermal neurofibromas—requires inactivation of the normal *NF1* allele in somatic cells, a process known as **loss of heterozygosity**. This two-hit mechanism is characteristic of **tumor suppressor genes**, as seen in other inherited cancer predisposition syndromes like retinoblastoma and Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Tumor formation occurs when both copies of the gene are inactivated: the first by an inherited mutation, the second by a somatic mutation.

## <mark>Perineural Spread</mark>

<mark>A higher incidence of perineural spread has been reported in some studies, with Leibovitch et al.</mark> <mark>noting involvement in more than 50 percent of periocular basal cell carcinomas (BCCs), often leading to orbital invasion.</mark> <mark>These aggressive tumors frequently require extensive surgical intervention, including orbital exenteration in severe cases.</mark> <mark>Perineural spread may present clinically with pain, paresthesias, muscle weakness, or paralysis.</mark> <mark>The presence of focal neurologic symptoms at the site of a previously treated skin cancer should raise suspicion for nerve involvement.</mark>

## <mark>Metastasis</mark>

<mark>Metastasis of BCC is rare, occurring in only 0.0028 to 0.55 percent of cases.</mark> <mark>Lymph node and lung involvement are the most common sites of metastatic spread.</mark> <mark>In a series by Von Domarus et al., three out of five patients with metastatic BCC had histologic evidence of perineural or intravascular invasion.</mark> <mark>Squamous differentiation was not seen in the primary tumors but was present in two of the five metastatic cases.</mark> <mark>Overall, squamous differentiation was observed in 15 percent of primary or metastatic tumors among 170 reviewed cases.</mark> <mark>Aggressive histologic features—such as morpheaform growth pattern, squamous metaplasia, and perineural invasion—are recognized risk factors for metastasis.</mark>

## <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

Diagnosis of BCC is based on accurate histopathologic interpretation of skin biopsy specimens. Shave biopsy is often sufficient and preferred; a sterilized razor blade allows precise control over biopsy depth and is frequently superior to a No. 15 scalpel for this technique. Punch biopsy is particularly useful for evaluating flat lesions, such as morpheaform BCC, or recurrent tumors arising within a scar.

## <mark>Histopathology</mark>

<mark>Histopathologic features vary by subtype, but most BCCs share common characteristics.</mark> <mark>The malignant basaloid cells typically have large nuclei with scant cytoplasm.</mark> <mark>Despite nuclear enlargement, overt nuclear atypia may be minimal, and mitotic figures are usually rare or absent.</mark> <mark>A hallmark feature is stromal retraction around tumor nests, creating peritumoral lacunae, which aids in diagnosis.</mark>

### Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma

Nodular BCC is the most common subtype, accounting for approximately 50 percent of cases. It is characterized by well-circumscribed nodules of basophilic tumor cells and prominent stromal retraction (Fig. 115-8A). Micronodular BCC refers to tumors composed of multiple small nodules less than 15 μm in diameter (Fig. 115-8B), which may have a higher risk of recurrence due to less distinct margins.

### Pigmented Basal Cell Carcinoma

Pigmented BCC shares histologic features with nodular BCC but includes melanin deposition. Melanocytes are found interspersed among tumor cells and contain abundant melanin granules in their cytoplasm and dendrites. While tumor cells themselves contain little melanin, the surrounding stroma often harbors numerous melanophages. Although about 75 percent of BCCs contain melanocytes, significant pigmentation is present in only about 25 percent of cases.

### Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma

Superficial BCC is characterized by small buds of malignant basaloid cells extending from the epidermal basal layer into the upper dermis. The peripheral cells typically show palisading, and epidermal atrophy may be present. Dermal invasion is usually minimal. This subtype is most commonly found on the trunk and extremities but can also occur on the head and neck.

# <mark>Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma</mark>

<mark>Superficial basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is characterized microscopically by buds of malignant basaloid cells extending from the basal layer of the epidermis into the upper dermis.</mark> <mark>The peripheral cells typically show palisading.</mark> Epidermal atrophy may be present, and dermal invasion is usually minimal. This subtype is most commonly found on the trunk and extremities, although it can also occur on the head and neck. A chronic inflammatory infiltrate is often present in the upper dermis.

# Morpheaform Basal Cell Carcinoma

Morpheaform (or infiltrative) BCC consists of thin strands or cords of tumor cells embedded within a dense fibrous stroma. The tumor cells are closely packed and may be as narrow as a single cell in thickness. These strands extend deeply into the dermis, often beyond the clinically apparent margins, making the tumor larger than it appears on physical examination. Recurrent BCCs may also exhibit similar infiltrative patterns within scar tissue.

# Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus

Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (FEP) is a variant of BCC that presents histologically as long, interwoven strands of basaloid cells within a fibrous stroma. It shares features with both reticulated seborrheic keratoses and superficial BCC, making diagnosis dependent on careful histologic evaluation.

# Differential Diagnosis

## Nodular BCC
- Dermal nevus  
- Squamous cell carcinoma  
- Appendageal tumor  
- Dermatofibroma  
- Scar  
- Seborrheic keratosis  

## Pigmented BCC
- Nodular melanoma  
- Superficial spreading melanoma  
- Lentigo maligna melanoma  
- Appendageal tumor  
- Compound nevus  
- Blue nevus  

## Superficial BCC
- Bowen disease  
- Mammary or extramammary Paget disease  
- Superficial spreading melanoma  
- Single plaque of psoriasis  
- Single plaque of eczema  

## Morpheaform BCC
- Scar  
- Morphea  
- Trichoepithelioma  

## Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus
- Skin tag  
- Papillomatous dermal nevus  
- Fibroma  

# Treatment

Management of BCC depends on anatomic location, tumor subtype, and histologic features. Treatment options include Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS), standard surgical excision, destructive modalities (e.g., curettage and desiccation, cryotherapy), radiotherapy, and topical chemotherapy.

The best chance for cure is with appropriate initial treatment of primary BCC, as recurrent tumors are more likely to recur again and cause extensive local tissue destruction. An algorithmic approach to management should be followed based on risk stratification.

## Mohs Micrographic Surgery (See Chap. 245)

Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) provides superior margin control compared to standard excision, allowing for maximal tissue preservation while achieving high cure rates. Studies report a recurrence rate of **1%** for primary BCCs treated with MMS, significantly lower than other modalities:
- Standard excision: 10%  
- Curettage and desiccation (C&D): 7.7%  
- Radiotherapy (XRT): 8.7%  
- Cryotherapy: 7.5%  

For recurrent BCCs, MMS has a recurrence rate of **5.6%**, again outperforming:
- Excision: 17.6%  
- XRT: 9.8%  
- C&D: 40%  

MMS is the treatment of choice for morpheaform BCC, poorly demarcated tumors, incompletely excised lesions, and other high-risk cases.

# <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS</mark>

## <mark>Presentation</mark>

<mark>The presence of any friable, non-healing lesion should raise the suspicion of skin cancer.</mark> Frequently, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is diagnosed in patients who report that the lesion bled briefly, then healed completely, only to recur later. <mark>BCC typically develops on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck but can occur anywhere on the body.</mark> <mark>Common features include translucency, ulceration, telangiectasias, and a rolled border.</mark> Clinical characteristics vary among sub-types, which include nodular, superficial, morpheaform (sclerosing), pigmented BCC, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (FEP).

## Basal Cell Carcinoma Sub-Types

### Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma

Nodular BCC is the most common clinical sub-type (Fig. 115-1). It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck and presents as a translucent papule or nodule, depending on duration. Telangiectasias are commonly present, and the lesion often has a rolled border. Larger lesions with central necrosis are historically referred to as rodent ulcers (Fig. 115-2). The differential diagnosis includes traumatized dermal nevus and amelanotic melanoma.

### Pigmented Basal Cell Carcinoma

Pigmented BCC is a variant of nodular BCC characterized by increased melanization. It appears as a hyperpigmented, translucent papule and may be eroded (Fig. 115-3). The differential diagnosis primarily includes nodular melanoma.

### Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma

Superficial BCC most commonly occurs on the trunk and presents as an erythematous, well-demarcated patch that may resemble eczema (Fig. 115-4). An isolated patch of "eczema" that fails to respond to topical treatment should prompt suspicion for superficial BCC.

### Morpheaform (Sclerosing) Basal Cell Carcinoma

Morpheaform BCC is an aggressive variant with distinct clinical and histologic features. Lesions often have an ivory-white appearance and may resemble a scar or a small, indurated plaque (Fig. 115-5). This sub-type is more infiltrative and has a higher risk of recurrence.

## <mark>Polymorphous Light Eruption (PMLE)</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Features</mark>

#### <mark>History</mark>
Polymorphous light eruption (PMLE) typically presents in the first three decades of life and affects females two to three times more frequently than males. It occurs across all skin types and racial groups but is more prevalent in Caucasians. Approximately 20% of patients report a positive family history, suggesting a genetic predisposition.

<mark>The eruption usually appears each spring or during sunny vacations, following the first significant ultraviolet radiation (UVR) exposure after a period of minimal sun exposure.</mark> <mark>It may also be triggered by recreational sunbed use or, very rarely, by visible light.</mark> <mark>The condition often diminishes with continued sun exposure throughout the season—a phenomenon known as "hardening" or desensitization.</mark> PMLE is uncommon in winter unless exposure occurs via UVR reflected from snow or transmitted through window glass.

Individual susceptibility varies. The time between UVR exposure and onset of lesions ranges from hours to days, typically not less than 30 minutes (though itching may precede visible changes). Lesions resolve completely within days to one or two weeks after exposure ends, without scarring. Recurrent outbreaks in the same individual tend to affect the same sun-exposed areas symmetrically, although only some exposed skin is usually involved—particularly areas that are typically covered during winter. Large portions of exposed skin may remain unaffected.

An extreme variant, **juvenile spring eruption**, primarily affects boys in spring and is characterized by pruritic papules and vesicles localized to the ear helices; typical PMLE may coexist. Systemic symptoms such as malaise or nausea are rare but possible in isolated cases.

#### <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>
<mark>PMLE exhibits a wide range of morphologic presentations, all sharing similar pathogenesis and prognosis.</mark> <mark>Common forms include:</mark>
- <mark>**Papular**</mark>
- <mark>**Papulovesicular**</mark>
- <mark>**Plaque-like**</mark>

<mark>Lesions are pruritic, erythematous, and symmetrically distributed, primarily affecting sun-exposed sites.</mark> <mark>The rash develops within hours of UVR exposure and resolves fully over several days to two weeks.</mark>

### Pathogenesis
PMLE is very likely a genetically determined **delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) reaction** directed against UVR-induced cutaneous antigens. Histologically, it shows **epidermal spongiosis** with a **dermal perivascular infiltrate** composed predominantly of mononuclear cells and associated edema.

The specific radiation-absorbing molecules that initiate PMLE have not been identified, but multiple candidates may be involved, varying between and within individuals. Potential mechanisms include:
- Direct antigenicity of UVR-altered molecules
- Free radical-mediated modification of nearby cellular components to form neoantigens  
Both mechanisms may contribute.

Repeated sunlight exposure induces cutaneous immunologic tolerance, which may suppress the underlying DTH response—explaining the progressive desensitization ("hardening") observed as summer progresses or during prophylactic phototherapy.

### Ultraviolet Radiation Sensitivity
UVA radiation (315–400 nm) is generally more effective than UVB (280–315 nm) in triggering PMLE. Studies show:
- UVA elicits the eruption in approximately **56%** of patients
- UVB in about **17%**
- Combined UVA/UVB in **27%**

Other reports suggest UVB sensitivity may occur in up to **57%** of patients. Overall:
- ~**50%** of PMLE patients are sensitive to UVB
- ~**75%** are sensitive to UVA
- ~**25%** react to both

Visible light may rarely play a role.

Notably, many sunscreens block UVB effectively but transmit UVA, potentially leading to a **paradoxical worsening** of PMLE despite sunscreen use.

### Management
PMLE responds to:
- **Broad-spectrum sunscreens** (with strong UVA protection)
- **Short-term topical or oral corticosteroids**
- **Prophylactic low-dose immunosuppressive phototherapy** (e.g., narrowband UVB or UVA) initiated in spring for individuals with frequent recurrences

This prophylactic approach leverages the natural development of tolerance, reducing symptom severity over time.

## <mark>Clinical Features of PMLE</mark>

<mark>In any given patient, polymorphic light eruption (PMLE) outbreaks tend to affect the same exposed skin sites consistently, usually in a symmetric pattern.</mark> <mark>The extent of involvement may gradually spread or recede over time.</mark> Not all sun-exposed skin is affected—typically, only certain areas develop lesions, often those that are intermittently exposed or normally covered. Large regions of exposed skin may remain spared.

An extreme example is **juvenile spring eruption**, which primarily affects boys in the spring and presents with pruritic papules and vesicles localized to the ear helices. In some cases, typical PMLE may coexist.

Systemic symptoms are rare in PMLE, but isolated reports include malaise, nausea, and other nonspecific sensations.

## <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>

<mark>PMLE exhibits a wide range of morphologic presentations, all likely sharing similar pathogenesis and prognosis.</mark> <mark>Described forms include:</mark>

- <mark>**Papular** (most common)</mark>
- <mark>**Papulovesicular**</mark>
- <mark>**Plaque**</mark>
- <mark>**Vesiculobullous**</mark>
- <mark>**Insect bite-like**</mark>
- <mark>**Erythema multiforme-like**</mark>

<mark>Pruritus without visible lesions may rarely occur, but a macular variant has not been clearly documented.</mark>

<mark>The **papular form** is characterized by small or large, discrete or confluent lesions that often cluster.</mark> <mark>This is followed in frequency by the papulovesicular and plaque types; other forms are uncommon.</mark>

An **eczematous variant** has been reported, but such cases likely represent mild chronic actinic dermatitis or photo-exacerbated seborrheic or atopic eczema rather than true PMLE.

<mark>Different morphologic variants can occur simultaneously at different body sites in the same individual.</mark> <mark>For example, diffuse facial erythema and swelling may accompany typical papular lesions elsewhere.</mark>

A variant known as **benign summer light eruption**, recognized in continental Europe, refers to small papular PMLE that spares the face and develops after several days of continued sun exposure.

## <mark>Laboratory Tests</mark>

### <mark>Histology</mark>

<mark>Histopathologic findings in PMLE are characteristic but not pathognomonic and vary with lesion morphology.</mark> <mark>Common features include:</mark>

- <mark>Moderate to dense **perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate** in the upper and mid dermis</mark>
- <mark>Predominance of **T cells**, with occasional neutrophils and rare eosinophils</mark>
- <mark>**Upper dermal and perivascular edema**</mark>
- <mark>**Endothelial cell swelling**</mark>

<mark>Epidermal changes may be absent or include:</mark>

- <mark>Variable **spongiosis**</mark>
- <mark>Occasional **dyskeratosis**</mark>
- <mark>**Exocytosis** of lymphocytes</mark>
- <mark>**Basal cell vacuolization**</mark>

### Blood Tests

Recommended laboratory evaluations include:

- **Antinuclear antibody (ANA)** and **extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) antibody** testing to exclude subacute cutaneous or other forms of lupus erythematosus
- **Red blood cell protoporphyrin** measurement if erythropoietic protoporphyria is suspected, particularly in cases with diagnostic uncertainty

### <mark>Phototesting</mark>

- <mark>**Monochromator phototesting** confirms photosensitivity in up to 50% of PMLE cases but lacks specificity for distinguishing PMLE from other photodermatoses.</mark>
- <mark>**Provocation testing** using a solar simulator or broadband light source—sometimes repeated over 2–3 consecutive days—can often reproduce the eruption. This may aid diagnosis and allow biopsy when clinical and historical features are inconclusive.</mark>

## Differential Diagnosis

See Box 90-1.

## Complications

While most patients with PMLE do not develop other systemic diseases, a small subset may go on to develop **lupus erythematosus**. Additionally, there is an increased prevalence of prior PMLE among patients diagnosed with lupus, suggesting a possible association between the two conditions.

# <mark>Laboratory Studies</mark>

<mark>Unless the diagnosis is certain, important investigations for all photosensitive conditions include assessment of circulating anti-nuclear factor and extractable nuclear antibody titers, as well as blood, urine, and stool porphyrin concentrations.</mark> <mark>Lesional histologic features are characteristic in many photodermatoses—particularly polymorphic light eruption (PMLE), hydroa vacciniforme (HV), and chronic actinic dermatitis (CAD)—but are rarely diagnostic except in HV.</mark> Direct immunofluorescence may assist in diagnosing cutaneous lupus.

<mark>Phototesting of normal back skin using a monochromator in CAD and solar urticaria (SU) often reproduces the papules or wheals typical of the condition, frequently at low irradiation doses, and helps define the action spectrum of the eruption.</mark> <mark>In xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), phototesting typically shows delayed erythema developing over 2–3 days with an abnormally low dose threshold, often progressing to blistering.</mark> <mark>However, phototesting is only moderately reliable in other photodermatoses, although solar-simulating or broadband irradiation may help induce the rash to support diagnosis.</mark>

<mark>In eczematous photosensitivity, patch and photopatch testing are essential to identify potential inducing or exacerbating allergens.</mark> For certain genophotodermatoses, specialized techniques such as assessment of DNA excision repair or RNA synthesis recovery rate in cultured patient fibroblasts after ultraviolet radiation (UVR) exposure are required for definitive diagnosis.

## Phototesting

The use of phototesting in clinical dermatology varies widely between countries and centers. While it is the investigation of choice when the diagnosis of a photodermatosis is uncertain or when details of the action spectrum are needed, it remains primarily a research tool available at only a limited number of clinical centers.

Phototesting in suspected photodermatosis falls into two main categories:
- **Monochromatic phototesting**: Performed on the upper back at a series of wavelengths and doses to elicit the eruption and identify the action spectrum.
- **Photoprovocation testing**: Uses a broad-spectrum source to induce the eruption for clinical diagnosis or biopsy when necessary.

Monochromatic phototesting is best conducted with a xenon arc irradiation monochromator for precise determination of wavelength dependency. Photoprovocation testing is most effectively performed with a solar simulator—a filtered xenon arc source that closely mimics natural sunlight at noon during midsummer in temperate regions. Alternative protocols using filtered metal halide or fluorescent light sources are also acceptable. Sunlight with filters has been used in some settings, but its variability makes it unsuitable for routine clinical use.

Monochromatic testing should be performed on unaffected skin of the upper back, lateral to the paravertebral groove. Lesion induction—except in conditions like SU and CAD, where monochromatic testing readily provokes lesions—is best achieved with broadband sources over larger areas of skin known to be susceptible. Conditions such as PMLE, actinic prurigo (AP), and HV often require repeated irradiation with UVA, UVB, or combined sources to reproduce the characteristic skin changes.

### Precautions and Standardization

To avoid false-negative results, potent topical and systemic corticosteroids should be discontinued for several days prior to testing if possible. The effect of oral immunosuppressive agents on test outcomes is less clear, but these should also ideally be withheld. False-positive results may occur in patients with widespread active disease; therefore, the eruption should be well-controlled before testing, ideally by maintaining the patient in a low-light environment.

However, these optimal conditions are often difficult to achieve during active eruptions, and testing may proceed with the understanding that results could be unreliable.

All phototesting must be performed using standardized, sequentially increasing doses (often in a geometric series) and wavelengths. Results should be read at consistent time points post-exposure under controlled environmental conditions of light and temperature to ensure accuracy and reproducibility.

## Public Health Dermatology: Examples and Impact

Although current dermatologic research remains largely focused on cellular and sub-cellular levels of analysis, meaningful progress in public health dermatology demonstrates the power of population-level interventions.

<mark>A landmark example is the study by Taplin and colleagues on scabies among the Kuna Indians in the San Blas Archipelago off Panama.</mark> <mark>In the 1980s, scabies affected a large proportion of children, causing significant suffering and frequent secondary bacterial infections.</mark> <mark>Despite using available treatments, the burden of disease remained high.</mark> <mark>A dramatic decline—from approximately 33% to 1%—was achieved only when a public health strategy was implemented: mass treatment of entire communities, regardless of symptom status.</mark> 

<mark>Similar success was seen in the Solomon Islands, where population-wide ivermectin administration reduced scabies prevalence from 25% to 1%, along with marked decreases in pyoderma and likely post-streptococcal nephritis.</mark>

<mark>Another major initiative is the Global Alliance to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis, a collaboration between the World Health Organization, national ministries of health, and private sector partners.</mark> <mark>This campaign, aimed at eradicating a debilitating disease, became one of the fastest-growing public health programs in history.</mark> <mark>By 2000, it had treated 25 million people across 12 countries; by 2004, this expanded to 250 million people in 39 countries.</mark> <mark>The program goes beyond mass drug administration, incorporating public education and guidance on skin care for lymphedema to reduce long-term complications.</mark>

<mark>Public health dermatology also includes non-pharmaceutical strategies.</mark> <mark>Skin cancer prevention campaigns promoting reduced ultraviolet exposure have been widely implemented.</mark> <mark>In Mali, a training program for general health workers in basic dermatologic care significantly improved patient outcomes.</mark> <mark>The proportion of patients receiving a correct diagnosis and appropriate treatment rose from 42% before training to 81% afterward.</mark> <mark>These gains persisted for at least 18 months.</mark> <mark>Notably, prescription costs fell by 25%, suggesting prior overuse of inappropriate empirical treatments.</mark> <mark>Similar inefficiencies in resource use for skin conditions like scabies and pyoderma have been documented in Mexico.</mark>

<mark>Ryan highlighted the impact of educational clinics in Tanzania, where targeted programs help prevent and manage skin cancer in a high-risk albino population of 170,000, emphasizing early detection and treatment.</mark>

<mark>While such interventions may lack the "high-tech" appeal of biologic therapies targeting specific receptors, they often deliver greater population-level benefit.</mark> <mark>The principle is clear: a small benefit applied widely can outweigh a large benefit given to only a few.</mark> <mark>Low-technology, scalable solutions can thus generate substantial public health gains.</mark>

### Future of Public Health in Dermatology

Some dermatologists have moved beyond hospital-based care to conduct population-level needs assessments and organize services accordingly. International collaborations are increasingly focused on reducing the global burden of skin disease through strategic planning and targeted programs.

Organizations such as the International Foundation for Dermatology and the International League of Dermatological Societies are leading these efforts, particularly in developing countries. Their work emphasizes improving community dermatology programs, enhancing diagnostic accuracy, and providing evidence-based management guidelines for common skin conditions.

Training initiatives—such as those at the Regional Dermatology Training Centre in Moshi, Tanzania, and short courses in Guerrero, Mexico, and Mali—are designed to build local capacity. A core objective is training primary care providers who can then disseminate knowledge within their own communities, creating a multiplier effect in improving dermatologic care worldwide.

# General principles of treatment

Ten new clinical trials on scabies treatment have been published since the previous guideline in 2010. Recent data focus on mass population treatment, usually with ivermectin. Based on comparative studies evaluating the efficacy of different antiscabetic treatments, a distinction is made between 'recommended' and 'alternative' treatments. The availability of antiscabetic drugs varies across European countries, leading to variability in treatment choices in practice.

<mark>Topical treatment should be applied to all skin areas, including the scalp, groin, navel, external genitalia, finger and toe web spaces, and beneath the nails.</mark> <mark>It should be applied at night and left in place for 8–12 hours.</mark> <mark>The skin should be cool and dry before application.</mark> <mark>A second application is recommended after 7–14 days.</mark> After treatment, patients should change into clean clothing. All close personal contacts of the patient should be treated simultaneously to prevent re-infestation.

Clothing, bedding, towels, and other personal items should be machine washed at 50°C or higher, dry-cleaned, or sealed in a plastic bag for 1 week.

Patients should receive a detailed explanation of their infestation along with clear written information.

The infestation is considered cleared if, 1 week after completion of treatment, there are no signs of active scabies (i.e., no new lesions or nocturnal pruritus). Post-treatment itching may persist for 2–4 weeks.

# Recommended treatments

- <mark>**Permethrin 5% cream**: Apply from head to toe and wash off after 8–12 hours. Repeat treatment after 7–14 days {evidence level Ib; grade A recommendation}.</mark>  
- <mark>**Oral ivermectin**: 200 micrograms/kg, taken with food, given as two doses 1 week apart {evidence level Ib; grade A recommendation}.</mark>

- **Lindane**: No longer recommended due to risk of neurotoxicity.

# Crusted scabies

- **Topical scabicide** (permethrin 5% cream or benzyl benzoate 25% lotion): Apply daily for 7 days, then twice weekly until cure, **and**  
- **Oral ivermectin**: 200 micrograms/kg on days 1, 2, and 8.

## <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

<mark>Lichen sclerosus (LSc) is discussed in detail in Chap.</mark> 63. The symptoms and signs of male genital LSc are summarized in Table 75-3 and partially illustrated in Figs. 75-15 and 75-16. <mark>The classic genital morphologic presentation of LSc is atrophic white patches or plaques.</mark> <mark>However, lilac, slightly scaly patches with telangiectasia and sparse purpura—similar to the classic clinical manifestations of extragenital LSc—may also be observed.</mark> <mark>Urethral involvement may be more common and extensive than previously recognized.</mark>

<mark>Most cases of LSc can be diagnosed clinically.</mark> <mark>If there is diagnostic uncertainty, a biopsy should be performed.</mark> The histologic findings are discussed in Chap. 63.

## DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Disorders from which LSc must be differentiated are listed in Box 75-6.

## COMPLICATIONS

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the penis is the most concerning complication of LSc. A transformation rate between 4% and 9.5% has been reported, with a latent period of 10 to 30 years. Glans involvement with LSc is a significant risk factor. Carcinoma complicating LSc accounts for approximately 25% to 50% of all penile cancer cases. A pseudohyperplastic preputial SCC associated with LSc has been described; this variant is an extremely well-differentiated, non-verruciform, often multicentric form of SCC.

Treatment of LSc is discussed in Chap. 63 and in online resources.

---

## Non-Specific Balanoposthitis

Non-specific balanoposthitis is considered either a diagnosis of exclusion or a descriptive term reflecting limitations in diagnostic precision. Sexually transmitted infections, immunosuppression, diabetes, and primary dermatoses such as psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, Zoon balanitis (ZB), lichen sclerosus (LSc), lichen planus (LP), genital warts, or carcinoma in situ must be ruled out. A biopsy is essential for accurate diagnosis.

In approximately 10% of biopsy specimens from patients presenting with balanoposthitis, non-specific histopathologic features are found. While genitourinary physicians often diagnose candidiasis, dermatologists argue that *Candida* infection typically complicates existing inflammatory mucocutaneous conditions and represents a secondary, opportunistic phenomenon rather than a primary cause.

Preputial dysfunction is likely both a cause and consequence in most cases of non-specific balanoposthitis, and many patients may have undiagnosed LSc as the underlying condition. Treatment can be challenging, and the condition may not respond to local hygiene measures, soap substitution, topical steroids, or topical and systemic antibiotics.

The definitive treatment is circumcision, which is curative in most cases.

# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

The algorithm shown in Box 75-1 emphasizes the need to obtain a complete history, perform an adequate examination, and construct a differential diagnosis. <mark>Initiating investigations to exclude sexually transmitted disease or performing a biopsy may be indicated.</mark> <mark>Occasionally, a trial of treatment may help crystallize a diagnosis.</mark>

The responsibility for the elucidation of anogenital symptoms may need to be shared with the genitourinary physician, pediatrician, urologist, or colorectal surgeon.

## History

Although classic dermatologic symptoms (itch, rash, lumps or bumps, or ulceration) may be present, the physician must be alert to symptoms of sexually transmitted disease (e.g., discharge, dysuria) and urologic disease (e.g., pain, hematuria, dysuria), as well as male sexual dysfunction.

Symptomatic male sexual dysfunction equates with male dyspareunia—that is, painful or difficult sexual intercourse. Many men will not volunteer such information, so specific inquiry should be tactfully made. The components of normal male sexual function are libido, erection, ejaculation, and orgasm.

## Cutaneous Lesions

A systematic approach to the penis and prepuce is summarized in the algorithm (see Box 75-1). The foreskin should be gently retracted (if present), the gluteal and crural folds and the meatal lips parted, and the rectum examined digitally. Site, distribution, and morphology of lesions should be conventionally noted and analyzed.

Specific male genital signs include:
- **Phimosis**: non-retractable foreskin; this condition should be regarded as a sinister situation because it impedes complete inspection and palpation of the glans and coronal sulcus. Causes of phimosis are listed in Table 75-2.
- **Paraphimosis**: foreskin fixed in retraction; it is rarer and can result from vigorous sexual activity, acute contact urticaria, acute allergic contact dermatitis, or lichen sclerosus (LSc).
- **Balanitis**: inflammation of the glans penis.
- **Posthitis**: inflammation of the prepuce.
- **Dorsal perforation of the prepuce**: ulceration through the prepuce involving the glans and shaft, leaving the prepuce as an empty sleeve ventrally.

Balanitis and posthitis xerotica (obliterans) are terms sometimes used to describe the end stage of chronic balanitis and posthitis, characterized by scarring and atrophy.

# 2022 European guideline for the management of balanoposthitis

## Abstract

**Background:** This guideline updates the 2014 edition on the management of balanoposthitis. <mark>Balanoposthitis refers to inflammation of the glans penis and prepuce, with diverse causes including infections, dermatoses, and premalignant conditions.</mark>

<mark>**Objective:** To improve recognition of symptoms, signs, and complications of penile skin conditions and to provide evidence-based recommendations on diagnosis and treatment for selected common or significant conditions.</mark>

**Methods:** The previous guideline was revised based on a literature review, prioritizing evidence from randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews.

**Results:** Key updates include:
- <mark>Clearer management guidance for **Group A streptococcal infections**</mark>
- <mark>Updated recommendations for **lichen sclerosus**, including circumcision and supportive care to reduce recurrence of genital herpes and warts</mark>
- <mark>Additional treatment options for **Zoon’s balanitis (plasma cell balanitis)**</mark>
- Inclusion of **calcineurin inhibitors** in therapeutic strategies
- Emphasis on the **risk of premalignancy**
- Change in terminology from "premalignant conditions" to **Penile Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PeIN)**

**Conclusion:** Balanoposthitis has multiple etiologies. High-quality evidence specific to penile skin diseases remains limited for many conditions.

---

## Introduction

This guideline aims to assist clinicians in recognizing the symptoms, signs, and complications of penile skin disorders that may present across specialties such as dermatology, sexual health, and urology. It provides recommendations on diagnosis and management but is not a comprehensive review of all forms of balanoposthitis.

The guideline focuses on a selected group of conditions considered common or clinically significant, particularly those managed in dermato-venereology or sexual health settings, either independently or in collaboration with other specialists or primary care providers.

### Conditions covered:
- <mark>Candidal balanoposthitis</mark>  
- <mark>Anaerobic infection</mark>  
- <mark>Aerobic infection</mark>  
- <mark>Lichen sclerosus</mark>  
- <mark>Lichen planus</mark>  
- <mark>Zoon’s balanitis (plasma cell balanitis)</mark>  
- <mark>Psoriasis and circinate balanitis</mark>  
- <mark>Seborrheic dermatitis</mark>  
- <mark>Irritant/allergic eczema</mark>  
- <mark>Fixed drug eruptions</mark>  
- Pre-malignancy or suspected malignancy  

<mark>The guideline applies primarily to individuals aged 16 years and older.</mark>

---

## <mark>Aetiology</mark>

<mark>**Balanitis** refers to inflammation of the glans penis; **posthitis** refers to inflammation of the prepuce.</mark> <mark>When both are involved, the term **balanoposthitis** is used.</mark> <mark>It encompasses a range of unrelated conditions with similar clinical presentations affecting this anatomical site (see Table 1).</mark>

<mark>Balanitis is rare after circumcision, and preputial dysfunction often contributes to its development.</mark> <mark>Infections—particularly candidal—are frequently secondary to underlying inflammatory dermatoses.</mark>

<mark>Other less common dermatoses may also cause balanoposthitis but are not detailed in this guideline.</mark>

---

## <mark>General Management of the Patient with Balanoposthitis</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Features</mark>

<mark>Symptoms and signs vary by underlying cause.</mark> <mark>Specific features of individual conditions are described in their respective management sections.</mark>

### <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

- <mark>Balanitis and balanoposthitis are descriptive terms encompassing various unrelated conditions. Clinical appearance may be suggestive but is never pathognomonic.</mark>
- <mark>**Biopsy** is sometimes required to exclude pre-malignant or malignant disease, especially in persistent, treatment-resistant, or atypical cases.</mark>

#### <mark>Recommended diagnostic investigations in uncertain cases:</mark>
- <mark>Detailed **sexual history**, including assessment of sexual risk behaviors</mark>  
- <mark>**Full STI screening** (including HIV), guided by history and clinical presentation, in accordance with current guidelines</mark>  
  <mark>- **HSV nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)** if ulceration is present</mark>
